abstract: Beginning in the 1960s, researchers have understood that one of the unique properties of psychedelic drugs is that their effects are modified by the context in which they are taken (also known as their set and setting dependence). To date, 7 different studies have shown that critical period reopening is a shared property across psychedelic drugs, including ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and ibogaine. Moreover, the context dependence of psychedelics effects has been recapitulated for both MDMA and ketamine. Recently, Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026 (PMID: 42972049) have claimed that psilocybin does not reopen the social reward learning critical period, which the authors interpret as a failure to replicate previously published results. Here, we re-analyzed results across three published datasets (Nardou et al., Nature 2019; Nardou et al., Nature 2023; Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026) in order to compare the impact of dose, training regimen, and social context on the social conditioned place preference (social CPP) assay. Our analysis reveals that methodological modifications likely account for Lu and colleagues inability to reopen the social reward learning critical period with psilocybin. Nevertheless, because their results recapitulate previous findings that psychedelics effects are context dependent, they support rather than challenge the growing literature demonstrating that psychedelics reopen critical periods.
